prompt: What connection exists between portfolio diversification and how work is spread across your team?
suggestedConnection: Both are about how risks combine, not just individual items. A portfolio of 'safe' holdings that all move together isn't diversified; a team where every critical task sits with the same two people isn't resilient, even if each person is excellent.
otherAngles: Correlation: do your people fail in the same situations (e.g. all on day shift)?
Rebalancing: shifting work deliberately before overload, not after.

prompt: How might Goodhart's law apply to evaluating an AI system?
suggestedConnection: If you tune an AI system to pass a fixed test set, it can get better at the test without getting better at real customer questions. Evaluation sets need refreshing with real, recent cases — the same way SLA metrics need pairing with case review.
otherAngles: Keep a hidden hold-out set that nobody optimises against.
Track how often humans edit AI outputs, not just test scores.

prompt: What could a pre-mortem teach someone planning for retirement withdrawals?
suggestedConnection: Sequence-of-returns risk is about bad timing early on. A pre-mortem asks 'it went wrong — why?', which naturally surfaces 'a market fall right after I started withdrawing'. Naming it in advance leads to buffers rather than panic.
otherAngles: Both convert vague worry into specific scenarios.
Both work best before the plan starts, not during.

prompt: Could the IKEA effect bias a build-versus-buy decision?
suggestedConnection: Teams tend to overvalue what they built themselves. That can make an internal tool feel better than a comparable bought one, and make it harder to retire. Naming the bias helps you judge on evidence rather than authorship.
otherAngles: The same effect can make managers overvalue processes they designed.
Ask someone who didn't build it to evaluate it.

prompt: What links Chesterton's fence and root-cause analysis?
suggestedConnection: Both are about understanding why something exists before changing it. A process step that looks pointless may be the fix from a past incident; removing it without asking can re-open the original failure.
otherAngles: Keep a short 'why this exists' note on unusual process steps.

prompt: Where do anchoring and walk-away options meet?
suggestedConnection: An investor anchored on purchase price and a negotiator anchored on the other side's first number both lose sight of their real alternatives. Knowing your BATNA — or your actual reason for holding — loosens the anchor's grip.
otherAngles: Write your alternatives down before you see any number.
Ask: would I make this choice if I'd never seen the anchor?

prompt: What do quiet teams and confident AI answers have in common?
suggestedConnection: Both hide uncertainty behind a smooth surface. A team that never reports errors and an AI that never says 'I don't know' can both look reliable while carrying hidden mistakes. In both cases you design for uncertainty to be visible.
otherAngles: Reward people (and systems) for flagging doubt.
Treat 'no problems reported' as a question, not an answer.

prompt: What can queue maths tell a manager about burnout?
suggestedConnection: Little's law says work in progress equals arrival rate times time in the system. If arrivals rise and capacity doesn't, queues grow — and people absorb the gap with longer hours. Burnout is often a capacity equation showing up as a human symptom.
otherAngles: Track WIP per person, not just case counts.
Limiting WIP is a wellbeing intervention as well as an efficiency one.
